Why Open-Ended is Harder Than MCQ

In P5 Science, it is not enough to just know the answer—you must explain the scientific process step-by-step. Examiners are strictly looking for exact keywords like gains heat and water vapour rather than casual terms like 'gets hot' or 'steam'. Missing a single linking concept like rate of evaporation can cost you full marks even if your final conclusion is correct.

Common P5 Open-Ended Writing Mistakes

Examiners deduct marks for loose everyday language. Master these exact scientific phrases instead.

Mistake 1: Vague Condensation Source

What Students Write
"The water condensed on the cold glass."
water vapour
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"The water vapour condensed on the cooler glass surface."
water vapour
1/1 marks
The Fix: Always specify that WATER VAPOUR (the gas) condenses, not liquid water.

Mistake 2: Magic Missing Heat

What Students Write
"The sun makes the water evaporate faster."
gains heat
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"The water gains heat from the sun and evaporates faster."
gains heat
2/2 marks
The Fix: Evaporation and boiling MUST include the phrase 'gains heat'. Condensation and freezing MUST include 'loses heat'.

Mistake 3: The Coldness Trap

What Students Write
"The ice cubes release coldness into the water."
water loses heat
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"The water loses heat to the ice cubes."
loses heat
1/1 marks
The Fix: 'Coldness' cannot travel. Only HEAT travels, always from a warmer region to a cooler region.

Mistake 4: Area vs Amount

What Students Write
"It evaporated faster because it is spread out more."
exposed surface area
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"It evaporated faster because it has a larger exposed surface area."
exposed surface area
1/1 marks
The Fix: Examiners are scanning for the exact scientific term 'exposed surface area'. Do not use everyday words like 'spread out' or 'wider'.

Mistake 5: The "Rate Of" Omission

What Students Write
"The wind makes the water evaporate."
rate of
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"The wind increases the rate of evaporation of the water."
rate of evaporation
1/1 marks
The Fix: Water evaporates regardless of wind. Wind simply changes the SPEED at which it happens, so you must write 'rate of evaporation'.

Mistake 6: Forgetting Relative Temperatures

What Students Write
"Water vapour touches the glass and condenses."
cooler
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"Warmer water vapour touches the cooler glass surface and condenses."
cooler
1/1 marks
The Fix: Condensation ONLY happens if there is a temperature difference. You must state what is 'warmer' and what is 'cooler'.

Mistake 7: Gas Volume Misconception

What Students Write
"50cm3 of air is added so the volume becomes 250cm3."
compressed
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"The volume remains unchanged because air has no definite volume and can be compressed."
compressed
2/2 marks
The Fix: Gas always takes the volume of its container. Adding more gas just compresses it, it doesn't change the container's free volume.

Mistake 8: Missing the Final State

What Students Write
"The vapour lost heat and condensed on the mirror."
water droplets
1/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"The vapour lost heat and condensed into water droplets on the mirror."
water droplets
2/2 marks
The Fix: 'Condenses' is the action. You must also state what is FORMED at the end of the action (water droplets/mist/water).

Boiling vs Evaporation

Boiling
  • Occurs ONLY at a fixed temperature (100°C for pure water).
  • Occurs throughout the liquid (bubbles form).
  • Fast process.
Evaporation
  • Occurs at any temperature below the boiling point.
  • Occurs ONLY at the exposed surface area.
  • Slow process.
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Boiling occurs at a fixed temperature WHILE evaporation occurs at any temperature."
Why Students Confuse These: Both turn liquid water into gas (water vapour), so students assume they are the exact same process just with different names.

Good Conductor vs Poor Conductor of Heat

Good Conductor
  • Allows heat to flow through it quickly.
  • Examples: Iron, steel, copper (metals).
  • Used for cooking pots to gain heat fast.
Poor Conductor
  • Allows heat to flow through it slowly.
  • Examples: Air, plastic, wood.
  • Used to prevent objects from losing heat (keeping food hot) or gaining heat (keeping ice cold).
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Metal is a good conductor of heat and loses heat faster to the surroundings, WHEREAS plastic is a poor conductor of heat and loses heat slower."
Why Students Confuse These: Students think poor conductors trap "coldness". They actually just block HEAT from entering or leaving.

Mist inside Car vs Mist outside Car

Mist on INSIDE of window
  • Happens when it is cooler OUTSIDE the car (e.g. raining).
  • Warmer water vapour inside the car touches the cooler inner surface.
Mist on OUTSIDE of window
  • Happens when it is cooler INSIDE the car (e.g. aircon is blasting).
  • Warmer water vapour from the surrounding air outside touches the cooler outer surface.
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Warmer water vapour from [location] comes into contact with the cooler [inner/outer] surface of the glass..."
Why Students Confuse These: They blindly memorize "water vapour condenses on the cold glass" without checking WHICH side of the glass is actually colder based on the scenario temperatures.

Contraction vs Compression

Contraction
  • Caused by a change in temperature (losing heat).
  • Applies to solids, liquids, AND gases.
  • Particles lose energy and move closer.
Compression
  • Caused by physical force (pushing a plunger).
  • Applies ONLY to gases.
  • Solids and liquids CANNOT be compressed.
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"The gas contracted BECAUSE it lost heat to the freezer, WHEREAS the gas compressed BECAUSE the plunger was pushed down."
Why Students Confuse These: Both result in a "smaller volume of air", so students use the words interchangeably.

Linking Words

Use words like because, so that, and which causes to connect your evidence to your scientific reason. For comparison questions, always use whereas or but.
Trap 1: Condensation happens just because it's cold

Students think cold air or ice itself turns into mist.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Condensation ONLY happens when warmer water vapour hits a cooler surface. The temperature DIFFERENCE is required.

Always state BOTH 'warmer water vapour' and 'cooler surface'.
Trap 2: The white clouds from a kettle are steam

Students assume the white fog above boiling water is steam (gas).

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Steam is an invisible gas. The white clouds are liquid water droplets formed when the steam condenses.

If you can see it, it's liquid (water droplets). If you can't, it's gas (water vapour/steam).
Trap 3: Adding air changes the volume of a container

If a container is 300cm3 and you pump in 50cm3 of air, the volume of air becomes 350cm3.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Gas has no definite volume. It will always fill exactly the space available because it can be compressed.

Volume of gas = Volume of container minus Volume of liquids/solids inside.
Trap 4: Water stops evaporating at night

Students think the sun must be out for evaporation to happen.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Evaporation occurs at any temperature above 0°C and below 100°C. It just has a slower rate of evaporation at night.

Never write 'evaporation stops'. Write 'rate of evaporation decreases'.
Trap 5: Metals keep things cold because they are cold materials

Metals feel cold to the touch, so they must be good for keeping ice cold.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Metals are good conductors of heat. They conduct heat from the warmer surroundings INTO the cold ice quickly, melting it faster!

To keep things cold, you need a POOR conductor (like foam, air, or plastic).
Trap 6: Coldness flows out of the fridge

When you leave the fridge door open, the kitchen gets cold because coldness escapes.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

There is no such thing as coldness energy. The warm air in the kitchen loses heat to the cooler air in the fridge.

Heat ALWAYS flows from warmer to cooler. Period.
Trap 7: Ice melts immediately at room temperature

If you take ice out of the freezer (-10°C), it starts melting instantly.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The ice must first gain heat until it reaches exactly 0°C. Only THEN does it start to melt into water.

Temperature stays constant at 0°C during the melting process.
Trap 8: Water volume matters for evaporation rate

A deep bucket of water evaporates faster than a shallow puddle if the bucket has more water.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The volume of water does NOT affect the rate. Only the exposed surface area matters (along with wind and temperature).

A wide puddle has a larger exposed surface area than a deep bucket.

EXPLAIN The CER Method

Use when asked to explain an observation or how a setup works.

Observation + BECAUSE + Scientific Reason (Keywords)

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

The ice cubes took the longest time to melt BECAUSE Y is the poorest conductor of heat / heat flowed through Y the slowest. Hot food will lose heat the slowest to the surroundings.
What to AVOID:
Skipping the observation and just writing the concept.
Using casual words like 'gets cold' instead of 'loses heat'.

STATE Direct Fact

Use when asked to name, state, or identify without explaining.

Question Concept + Exact Scientific Term

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

Evaporation is a process where liquid (gains heat) and changes into gas at any temperature.
What to AVOID:
Writing a long explanation. You only get 1 mark, don't waste time.

DESCRIBE Step-by-Step Flow

Use when asked to describe a process, formation, or sequence of events.

Action 1 → Action 2 → Final Result

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

The water gained heat from the heat source and boiled to become steam. The steam rises and comes into contact with the cooler underside surface of the metal tray, loses heat and condenses to become water.
What to AVOID:
Jumping to the final state without showing the heat gain/loss step.
Using ambiguous terms like 'turns into' instead of 'condenses' or 'evaporates'.

COMPARE Side-by-Side

Use when asked to compare two setups, objects, or processes.

Object A Trait + WHEREAS/WHILE + Object B Trait

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

Material X on top of W is a better conductor of heat, so it conducts heat from W to the cooler surroundings more quickly... However, without X on top, W, which is a poorer conductor of heat, conducts heat from the flame to the surroundings more slowly...
What to AVOID:
Only describing one side (e.g. "X is a better conductor"). You MUST mention both.
Using 'it' instead of naming the objects.

SUGGEST Action + Reason

Use when asked to suggest a change to an experiment or real-world setup.

Suggested Action + BECAUSE/SO THAT + Scientific Principle

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

Leave gaps in between the tiles to allow room for expansion.
What to AVOID:
Suggesting something that changes the aim of the experiment entirely.
Suggesting a change without stating the underlying scientific reason.

GIVE_REASON Evidence to Conclusion

Use when justifying a choice or outcome.

Keyword Reason (Data) + THEREFORE + Consequence

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

F. F has a greater volume of water so it has more heat to cook the egg.
What to AVOID:
Just giving the choice (e.g. "Container F") without the reason.

Universal Open-Ended Answer Checklist

✓ Did I use the exact scientific keywords (e.g., 'gains heat', 'water vapour')?
✓ Did I state WHERE the heat is gained from or lost to?
✓ If it's condensation, did I specify WHICH surface is 'cooler'?
✓ If comparing, did I talk about both objects/setups?
✓ Did I explicitly mention 'rate of evaporation' instead of 'evaporates faster'?
✓ Did I check if the question wants me to use data from the table/graph?
